Abstract:
In political science, we often find ourselves interested in analyzing only the part of a document collection that is relevant to the subject, but not necessarily knowing which part of the whole corpus is related and which part isn't. This makes it difficult to extract the document parts that would be needed for analysis.
Insightful findings in political science often require researchers to analyze documents of a certain subject or type, yet these documents are usually contained in large corpora that do not distinguish between pertinent and non-pertinent documents. In contrast, we can find this kind of information if we can make use of other related information that is available. In our paper, we study unsupervised domain adaptation as an information source to learn to separate the pertinent from the non-pertinent documents in a given topic. We describe a novel way to use the documents that you have already classified into your corpus and a subset of documents with only labels in order to train. We call this new technique adaptive ensembling. We evaluate the performance on a number of different political corpora, and the method shows that it gives good results. The paper concludes with some discussion on the future and the possible applications.

generations.raw_text: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated degradation (ERAD) is a principal mechanism that targets ER- and co-translational misfolded proteins to the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) for retro-translocation from the ER and degradation. We found that the Sel1L-Hrd1 complex is required for a key checkpoint in B cell development. The paper reports that the Sel1L-Hrd1 ERAD complex has a critical requirement for the development of the pro-B to pre-B cell transition in mice and humans. It reports that this complex, via the degradation of the protein CMAH, is important for the generation of double strand DNA. In particular, Sel1L and Hrd1 are shown to be essential to allow CMAH to get inside the nucleus through a nuclear localization signal and then have its function, that is to deaminate and convert an adenosine into a deoxyguanosine. Without this Sel1L-Hrd1-mediated function the cells have a defect in generating double strand DNA that is required to have a B cell receptor on the cell surface. As a result, mice without Sel1L or Hrd1 cannot make mature B cells. Further, we also show that the absence of Hrd1 causes the B cells to be hypermethylated at promoter regions as well as to have increased global DNA methylation. Also, this causes to have a reduction in the expression of several genes, such as B cell receptor (B2), Cytokine receptor (IL4R) and others. Finally, the data also indicates that the Hrd1 is responsible, via the ER, for the regulation of gene expression.
